blocks.prompt: 6. How many 6-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9?
blocks.explanation:
All six digits are used in every number; three digits each appear twice.
Plan: treat the digits like letters of a word with repeats and use the formula for objects not all different.
steps:
Given: the digits 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9.
To find: how many 6-digit numbers use all of them.
Method: \(\dfrac{n!}{n_1!\,n_2!\,n_3!}\) with \(n = 6\) and \(n_1 = n_2 = n_3 = 2\).

Count the repeats
\[n = 6,\quad 7 \to 2,\ 8 \to 2,\ 9 \to 2\]
Why: Each of 7, 8 and 9 appears twice.

Apply the formula
\[\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!} = \dfrac{720}{8} = 90\]
Why: Swapping the two 7s, the two 8s or the two 9s gives the same number, so each number was counted 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times. No digit is 0, so every arrangement is a genuine 6-digit number.

Check
\[\text{first digit 7: } \dfrac{5!}{1!\,2!\,2!} = 30\]
\[30 \times 3 = 90 \;\checkmark\]
Why: By symmetry 30 numbers start with each of 7, 8 and 9. A computer listing also gives 90.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(360\). That is \(\dfrac{6!}{2!}\), which divides by only one \(2!\). All three digits 7, 8 and 9 are repeated twice, so the correct answer is \(\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!\,2!} = 90\).
